message.content:
Below are several common ways you can pull *detailed* information for a specific network interface, depending on what platform or protocol you’re working with: | Platform / Protocol | Typical Command / Call | What it returns (key fields) | |---------------------|------------------------|------------------------------| | **Cisco IOS / IOS‑XE** | `show interface `
e.g., `show interface GigabitEthernet0/1` | • Interface status (up/down)
• MAC address
• MTU, speed, duplex
• Input/output counters (bytes, packets, errors, discards)
• Physical layer details (line protocol, link type, physical media) | | **Cisco NX‑OS** | `show interface `
or `show interface description` | Same as above plus additional NX‑OS‑specific fields such as “Interface State” and “Link Type”. | | **Juniper JUNOS** | `show interfaces detail`
or `show interfaces terse` + `show interfaces extensive` | • Operational state
• MAC address
• Speed, duplex, MTU
• Counters (in/out octets, packets, errors, discards)
• Physical attributes (media type, cable length). | | **Linux / Unix** | `ip -s link show ` or `ifconfig -a` | • Link flags (UP/DOWN, RUNNING)
• MAC address
• MTU, speed (via ethtool), duplex
• Statistics (rx/tx bytes, packets, errors, dropped, overruns). | | **Windows** | `Get-NetAdapterStatistics -Name ""` (PowerShell) | • Bytes received/transmitted
• Packets received/transmitted
• Errors, collisions, etc. | | **SNMP** | Walk OIDs under `IF-MIB::ifTable` (`.1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2`) | • `ifDescr`, `ifType`, `ifMtu`, `ifSpeed`, `ifPhysAddress`, `ifOperStatus`
• Counters: `ifInOctets`, `ifOutOctets`, `ifInErrors`, `ifOutErrors`, `ifInDiscards`, `ifOutDiscards`. | | **RESTCONF / NETCONF** | `>` (RESTCONF) or `` (NETCONF) | XML/JSON representation of the interface configuration and operational state, including all the same fields as the CLI but in machine‑readable form. | ### Quick Example – Cisco IOS ```bash Router# show interface GigabitEthernet0/1 GigabitEthernet0/1 is up, line protocol is up Hardware is Gigabit Ethernet, address is 001b.7c5f.9a01 (bia 001b.7c5f.9a01) MTU 1500 bytes, BW 1000000 Kbit/sec, DLY 10 usec, reliability 255/255, txload 1/255, rxload 1/255 Encapsulation ARPA, loopback not set Keepalive set (10 sec) Full-duplex, 1000Mb/s, media type is RJ45 ... 5 minute input rate 2000 bits/sec, 3 packets/sec 5 minute output rate 3000 bits/sec, 4 packets/sec 12345678 packets input, 987654321 bytes, 0 no buffer Received 0 broadcasts, 0 runts, 0 giants, 0 throttles 0 input errors, 0 CRC, 0 frame, 0 overrun, 0 ignored 87654321 packets output, 123456789 bytes, 0 underrun 0 output errors, 0 collisions, 0 interface resets ``` ### How to Use the Data 1. **Health Monitoring** – Track error counts (`ifInErrors`, `ifOutErrors`) over time; sudden spikes often indicate a bad cable or NIC issue. 2. **Performance Tuning** – Compare `ifInOctets` vs. `ifOutOctets` against the configured bandwidth (`ifSpeed`). If traffic approaches the limit, consider upgrading the link or load balancing. 3. **Troubleshooting** – Look at `ifInDiscards`/`ifOutDiscards` and `ifInDrop`/`ifOutDrop` to see if packets are being dropped due to congestion or misconfiguration. 4. **Capacity Planning** – Use historical statistics to forecast when a link will reach capacity. --- #### Want to Pull This Programmatically? If you’re writing a script or monitoring tool, you can automate the retrieval: - **Python + Netmiko** (for SSH CLI): ```python from netmiko import ConnectHandler device = { 'device_type': 'cisco_ios', 'host': '192.168.1.1', 'username': 'admin', 'password': 'pass', } net_connect = ConnectHandler(**device) output = net_connect.send_command('show interface GigabitEthernet0/1') print(output) ``` - **Python + PySNMP** (for SNMP): ```python from pysnmp.hlapi import * iterator = nextCmd( SnmpEngine(), CommunityData('public', mpModel=0), UdpTransportTarget(('192.168.1.1', 161)), ContextData(), ObjectType(ObjectIdentity('1.3.6.1.2.1.2.2.1.10.1')), # ifInOctets for ifIndex 1 ) for errorIndication, errorStatus, errorIndex, varBinds in iterator: if errorIndication: print(errorIndication) break else: for varBind in varBinds: print(f'{varBind[0]} = {varBind[1]}') ``` Feel free to let me know which platform or protocol you’re targeting, and I can drill down into more platform‑specific details or help you parse the output!
